title: Nehemiah 8:13–18
context: On the second day the heads of families, priests, and Levites gather to Ezra to study the law and find that the LORD commanded through Moses that Israel should live in booths during the feast of the seventh month (compare Leviticus 23:40–43). The people gather branches and build temporary shelters on roofs, in courtyards, in the courts of God’s house, and in the squares of the water gate and Ephraim’s gate. The narrator says that since the days of Joshua son of Nun the children of Israel had not done so, which interpreters commonly take to refer to the manner, scale, or joy of this observance, since Ezra 3:4 reports the feast of booths kept earlier; the exact sense is debated. Ezra reads from the law each day, the feast lasts seven days, and the eighth day is a solemn assembly. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about obedience flowing from the word, remembrance of God’s care in the wilderness, and great gladness.

verses.text: On the second day, the heads of fathers’ households of all the people, the priests, and the Levites were gathered together to Ezra the scribe, to study the words of the law.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the leaders, priests, and Levites gathering to Ezra on the second day to study the law. Leaders take responsibility to learn more deeply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the study session as the fruit of the first day’s reading (compare Ezra 7:10). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of continued learning from Scripture.

verses.text: They found written in the law how the LORD had commanded by Moses that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the leaders finding that the LORD commanded Israel to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month. Study leads to discovery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word guiding the people back to forgotten obedience (compare Leviticus 23:42). Both traditions commonly read the verse as Scripture shaping worship.

verses.text: and that they should publish and proclaim in all their cities and in Jerusalem, saying, “Go out to the mountain, and get olive branches, branches of wild olive, myrtle branches, palm branches, and branches of thick trees, to make temporary shelters, as it is written.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call to gather olive, myrtle, palm, and other branches to make temporary shelters, as it is written. Obedience follows quickly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the instructions as grounded in the written law. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that worship is shaped by God’s word rather than invention.

verses.text: So the people went out and brought them, and made themselves temporary shelters, everyone on the roof of his house, in their courts, in the courts of God’s house, in the wide place of the water gate, and in the wide place of Ephraim’s gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people building temporary shelters on roofs, in courtyards, and in public squares. The whole city becomes a place of remembrance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shelters as reminders of God’s care in the wilderness (compare Leviticus 23:43). Both traditions commonly read the verse as joyful, communal obedience.

verses.text: All the assembly of those who had come back out of the captivity made temporary shelters and lived in the temporary shelters, for since the days of Joshua the son of Nun to that day the children of Israel had not done so. There was very great gladness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see all who had returned from captivity living in shelters, with very great gladness. The narrator notes that nothing like it had been done since Joshua.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison with Joshua as highlighting the significance of the occasion. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact meaning of the comparison with caution, since Ezra 3:4 reports the feast kept earlier.

verses.text: Also day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read in the book of the law of God. They kept the feast seven days; and on the eighth day was a solemn assembly, according to the ordinance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra reading from the law each day of the feast, with a solemn assembly on the eighth day. Daily reading sustains the celebration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the feast kept according to the ordinance (compare Leviticus 23:36). Both traditions commonly read the verse as joining joy, worship, and the steady reading of God’s word.
